ormitory for three years, claiming the students would create noise pollution. Bike lanes in Oakland, San Diego and Los Angeles have faced lawsuits. Neighbors sued to block the construction of a food pantry in Alameda two years ago, saying it was on a “historic parking lot.” In San Jose in 2012, the owner of a gas station sued under CEQA when a competing gas station across the street attempted to add four new pumps, delaying the project for three years and costing its owner thousands of dollars in legal fees.
Work continues on UC Berkeley’s People's Park Housing Project in Berkeley, Calif., on Tuesday, Oct. 14, 2025. Neighbors in Berkeley delayed construction of a new UC dormitory there for three years, claiming the students would create noise pollution. (Jane Tyska/Bay Area News Group) Jane Tyska — Bay Area News Group
Critics, including Newsom and former Gov. Jerry Brown, have said CEQA has contributed to California’s housing shortage and high prices.
Last July, Newsom signed bills from Assemblywoman Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, and Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, to waive or streamline CEQA to build housing in already developed urban areas, and for other projects including farmworker housing, daycare centers, food banks and plants to build semiconductors, biotechnology and nanotechnology on land zoned for industrial uses.
“We needed to go bold and big on this holy grail reform,” Newsom said of the bills at the time.
Newsom has not taken a position on Proposition 45.
Wicks has endorsed it.
“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” she said at the Capitol Weekly Housing Conference in Sacramento on Feb. 24
Wicks cited a solar company that testified in a Sacramento hearing last year that it spent 12 years, filled out 11,000 pages of environmental studies and was required to obtain 72 permits from 28 agencies to get approval for one high-voltage electric transmission line.
“We say we have these climate goals, and yet we make it almost impossible to reach them,” Wicks said. “As Democrats, we have to have an honest conversation about what we’re doing here and where our values are. And for me, as a Democrat, government has to deliver results.”
Larry Gerston, a professor emeritus of political science at San Jose State University, said the measure involves two key California concerns: Environmental stewardship and housing costs.
“Californians are very environmentally inclined,” Gerston said. “We’ve seen it again and again. They have accepted higher costs in some cases to improve air quality and support other environmental rules. But it could be that people say, ‘We have to reduce costs in California, and this is one way to do it.’ I don’t know how it will go. There’s a lot at stake here.”

PUBLISHED: October 13, 2026 at 8:22 AM PDT | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 11:20 AM PST

Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
California’s richest are doing great. Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times. This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year. Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream — the highest 2% of earners — to keep paying their fair share while also helping the state avoid painful cuts to services induced by President Trump’s and House Republicans’ deliberately punitive H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Prop. 4 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)
Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections.
Prop. 5 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Prop. 37 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This measure looks great on the surface. But all that glitters isn’t gold. It would give builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it would artificially inflate the market by putting borrowed cash into buyers’ hands. Instead of lowering construction costs, this merely helps California home buyers take on more debt in the form of second mortgages.
Prop. 38 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/)
This deceptive ballot measure is an $8.4 billion money grab that would funnel taxpayer funds to a single private medical institute run by a billionaire, who is also the chief backer of the Proposition 38 campaign.
Prop. 39 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/15/endorsement-reject-proposition-39-voter-id-fraud-ballot-measure/)

# Endorsement: No on Prop. 45, leave state’s landmark environmental review law alone
...
Enter Proposition 45.
The ballot measure seeks to streamline the current CEQA process by giving agencies 365 business days to decide on the “report card” for projects the measures define as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation.
The measure also requires courts to resolve any cases within 270 calendar days.
The measure would limit public comment to 45 days and limit the scope of alternative projects — which typically arise as a result of the report card of mitigation measures — that must be analyzed in the review process.
...
The Press Democrat recognizes the need to reduce the red tape in development, both at the state and local levels.
But Prop.
45 is not the way to do it.
The Press Democrat recommends a no vote on Prop.
45.
Sure — the measure would tighten up the environmental review process: It would limit the number of alternative projects required to be studied, a move that takes away a public agency’s power and places it into the hands of the developer.

Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)

Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)

California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)

Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
California’s richest are doing great. Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times. This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year. Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream — the highest 2% of earners — to keep paying their fair share while also helping the state avoid painful cuts to services induced by President Trump’s and House Republicans’ deliberately punitive H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Prop. 4 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)
Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections.
Prop. 5 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Prop. 37 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This measure looks great on the surface. But all that glitters isn’t gold. It would give builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it would artificially inflate the market by putting borrowed cash into buyers’ hands. Instead of lowering construction costs, this merely helps California home buyers take on more debt in the form of second mortgages.
Prop. 38 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/)
This deceptive ballot measure is an $8.4 billion money grab that would funnel taxpayer funds to a single private medical institute run by a billionaire, who is also the chief backer of the Proposition 38 campaign.

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.

Article continues below this ad
But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.

Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don’t support it
By Joe Garofoli (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/joe-garofoli/) , Political Columnist Oct 21, 2026
Key CEQA reformers are concerned that Prop 45 could lead to more suburban sprawl.
Santiago Mejia/S.F. Chronicle
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to the state’s landmark environmental protection law either haven’t taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act.
CEQA was created in 1970 under then-Gov. Ronald Reagan to protect the beauty and vibrancy of the state. It requires developers to disclose potential environmental impacts of their projects and work with communities to blunt those impacts. Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don’t support it
By Joe Garofoli (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/joe-garofoli/) , Political Columnist Oct 21, 2026
Key CEQA reformers are concerned that Prop 45 could lead to more suburban sprawl.
Santiago Mejia/S.F. Chronicle
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to the state’s landmark environmental protection law either haven’t taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act.
CEQA was created in 1970 under then-Gov. Ronald Reagan to protect the beauty and vibrancy of the state. It requires developers to disclose potential environmental impacts of their projects and work with communities to blunt those impacts. But for decades, the law has been weaponized to jam development by everyone from NIMBYs to construction unions to wealthy suburbanites. A 2024 study (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Report279.pdf) by the Little Hoover Commission found that on average, “litigation adds almost two years to project time frames. In the face of such lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a project even if it would eventually have survived the CEQA process and been approved.” Preparing an environmental impact report can take a year or longer and cost up to $1 million.
Powerful labor interests have balked at changing CEQA, because unions have long used the law to extract wage concessions from developers. Wealthy suburbanites have used it to halt unwanted development. The same study found that 78% of CEQA litigation “may disproportionately challenge housing in higher-income neighborhoods.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 — backed by the California Chamber of Commerce, local chambers around the state, developers and affordable housing advocates — seeks to expedite development by imposing strict deadlines on certain categories of infrastructure projects described as “essential”: housing, water, clean energy, healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation.
Yet some key CEQA reformers are concerned about its unintended consequences, in particular that its provisions to loosen regulations could lead to more suburban sprawl — developments far from urban centers that destroy forest or agricultural land and force residents to drive everywhere, increasing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and exacerbating the climate crisis. Infill housing, meanwhile, is denser and typically enables residents to walk or take public transit to work. Many of California’s leading CEQA reformers oppose suburban sprawl and advocate for infill development, particularly near public transit.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, one of the architects of some of the Legislature’s most consequential CEQA reforms over the past decade, isn’t taking a position on the measure. Neither is one of his top allies, California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), which advocates for building more homes to ease California’s crippling housing crisis. Environmental advocate Tom Steyer supported (https://x.com/TomSteyer/status/1942757810686812370?s=20) CEQA reforms crafted in the Legislature but opposes (https://tomsteyer.substack.com/p/my-california-ballot-guide) Prop 45. It “goes way beyond any common-sense reforms to CEQA and is using the law to circumvent the public process and due process,” he wrote on Substack.
Other top Democrats have ducked taking a position.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
On Monday, when a reporter asked (https://x.com/joegarofoli/status/2112263830495810011?s=20) Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, about Prop 45, he spent nearly a minute talking about his support for Proposition 1, on affordable-housing bonds, before saying he “hasn’t weighed in on a lot of the other initiatives.” He said nothing about Prop 45.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has signed several key CEQA reform measures, announced his position on 12 of the 14 measures on the Nov. 3 ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), but not Props 45 or 42, one of two measures designed to invalidate Prop 40, the billionaire tax, if it passes.
Wiener told me he believes that CEQA is still in “serious need of reform.” And while he thinks Prop 45 “advances some very positive reforms like setting clear and firm timelines for permitting,” it also contains “problematic provisions like streamlining sprawl development.”
“As a result, I’m not taking a position on the measure,” he said.
Wiener is in a close race to succeed Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi in a San Francisco House race and may not want to further antagonize organized labor, which largely opposes Prop 45 and supports his opponent, Supervisor Connie Chan.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California YIMBY is focused on infill development, and its leaders say Prop 45 does little to help those projects.
“The reason we have no position is because it’s not a pure-play housing thing,” Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, told me. “We are CEQA reformers for housing, and we reformed CEQA for housing” through legislation.
Likewise, SPUR, the San Francisco nonprofit think tank that has supported other CEQA reforms, stopped short (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa) of backing Proposition 45 because it “would make broader changes that conflict with SPUR’s vision for urban growth. The measure could accelerate desirable projects, such as infill housing near transit and zero-emission energy infrastructure, but it could also streamline development that contributes to sprawl or environmental harm, including subdivisions on the urban edge and polluting energy facilities,” the organization wrote of its position, which is “No recommendation.”
In a sign of how the measure has scrambled traditional party loyalties, Prop 45 has even split California Republicans, who have long complained about regulations slowing housing production. Steve Hilton, the GOP candidate for governor who advocates building 10 more California cities, largely through the construction of single-family homes in sprawl-like developments, has said supportive things about Prop 45 but hasn’t taken a position. The California Republican Party has endorsed (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) Prop 45, but half a dozen local Republican Party groups oppose it, including the Marin County Republican Party.
Marin County Republican Party Chairman John Turnacliff said his members are worried that Prop 45 could lead to “crony capitalism.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“Let’s say some big data center developer comes in and takes care of some people in the Legislature with donations, and then all of a sudden they’re pushing for those guys to be qualified for this Proposition 45 benefit of not having to go through all the CEQA stuff, and then they get a fast-track deal,” Turnacliff said.
But other leading CEQA reformers are backing Prop 45, including Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, who wrote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/california-ceqa-20244075.php?utm_campaign=CMS%20Sharing%20Tools%20(Premium)&utm_source=share-by-email&utm_medium=email) a bill signed by Newsom last year that exempted most infill housing projects from the environmental reviews required under CEQA.
“What Prop 45 represents is a thoughtful way to actually get the projects (completed) that are essential for our communities,” Wicks told reporters Monday at a housing-related campaign event for Becerra in El Cerrito. “It still requires (projects) to go through CEQA. It just puts important shot clocks on it.”
Housing Action Coalition, another frequent ally on CEQA reform legislation, is also breaking ranks to back Prop 45. The organization felt that there were gaps in some recent reform legislation in Sacramento — like the ability to quickly build housing on parking lots at dilapidated shopping mall sites — that weren’t covered by existing legislation, said Ali Sapirman, the group’s advocacy and policy manager. Even though the Housing Action Coalition typically doesn’t support legislation that could lead to sprawl, it is confident that existing CEQA laws could be used to stop unwanted sprawl projects.
“And those gaps are real in terms of numbers,” Sapirman said. “The permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home, and that was really critical to our members.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But those gaps weren’t enough to convince other CEQA reformers to back Prop 45.
“There’s a bunch of stuff that 45 could do that we’re like, ‘Well, that would not be a great outcome,’” said California YIMBY’s Lewis. “But there’s some stuff that it would do that could be a good outcome. We weighed those against each other, and we were like, yeah, they kind of cancel each other out. We’re not going to weigh in on this one.”

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

I also want to see which major groups are against it, like the state Democratic Party and the Sierra Club, and whether the LA Times has weighed in.

Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don’t support it
By Joe Garofoli (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/joe-garofoli/) , Political Columnist Oct 21, 2026
Key CEQA reformers are concerned that Prop 45 could lead to more suburban sprawl.
Santiago Mejia/S.F. Chronicle
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to the state’s landmark environmental protection law either haven’t taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act.
CEQA was created in 1970 under then-Gov. Ronald Reagan to protect the beauty and vibrancy of the state. It requires developers to disclose potential environmental impacts of their projects and work with communities to blunt those impacts. But for decades, the law has been weaponized to jam development by everyone from NIMBYs to construction unions to wealthy suburbanites. A 2024 study (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Report279.pdf) by the Little Hoover Commission found that on average, “litigation adds almost two years to project time frames. In the face of such lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a project even if it would eventually have survived the CEQA process and been approved.” Preparing an environmental impact report can take a year or longer and cost up to $1 million.
Powerful labor interests have balked at changing CEQA, because unions have long used the law to extract wage concessions from developers. Wealthy suburbanites have used it to halt unwanted development. The same study found that 78% of CEQA litigation “may disproportionately challenge housing in higher-income neighborhoods.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 — backed by the California Chamber of Commerce, local chambers around the state, developers and affordable housing advocates — seeks to expedite development by imposing strict deadlines on certain categories of infrastructure projects described as “essential”: housing, water, clean energy, healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation.
Yet some key CEQA reformers are concerned about its unintended consequences, in particular that its provisions to loosen regulations could lead to more suburban sprawl — developments far from urban centers that destroy forest or agricultural land and force residents to drive everywhere, increasing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and exacerbating the climate crisis. Infill housing, meanwhile, is denser and typically enables residents to walk or take public transit to work. Many of California’s leading CEQA reformers oppose suburban sprawl and advocate for infill development, particularly near public transit.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, one of the architects of some of the Legislature’s most consequential CEQA reforms over the past decade, isn’t taking a position on the measure. Neither is one of his top allies, California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), which advocates for building more homes to ease California’s crippling housing crisis. Environmental advocate Tom Steyer supported (https://x.com/TomSteyer/status/1942757810686812370?s=20) CEQA reforms crafted in the Legislature but opposes (https://tomsteyer.substack.com/p/my-california-ballot-guide) Prop 45. It “goes way beyond any common-sense reforms to CEQA and is using the law to circumvent the public process and due process,” he wrote on Substack.
Other top Democrats have ducked taking a position.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
On Monday, when a reporter asked (https://x.com/joegarofoli/status/2112263830495810011?s=20) Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, about Prop 45, he spent nearly a minute talking about his support for Proposition 1, on affordable-housing bonds, before saying he “hasn’t weighed in on a lot of the other initiatives.” He said nothing about Prop 45.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has signed several key CEQA reform measures, announced his position on 12 of the 14 measures on the Nov. 3 ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), but not Props 45 or 42, one of two measures designed to invalidate Prop 40, the billionaire tax, if it passes.
Wiener told me he believes that CEQA is still in “serious need of reform.” And while he thinks Prop 45 “advances some very positive reforms like setting clear and firm timelines for permitting,” it also contains “problematic provisions like streamlining sprawl development.”
“As a result, I’m not taking a position on the measure,” he said.
Wiener is in a close race to succeed Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi in a San Francisco House race and may not want to further antagonize organized labor, which largely opposes Prop 45 and supports his opponent, Supervisor Connie Chan.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California YIMBY is focused on infill development, and its leaders say Prop 45 does little to help those projects.
“The reason we have no position is because it’s not a pure-play housing thing,” Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, told me. “We are CEQA reformers for housing, and we reformed CEQA for housing” through legislation.
Likewise, SPUR, the San Francisco nonprofit think tank that has supported other CEQA reforms, stopped short (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa) of backing Proposition 45 because it “would make broader changes that conflict with SPUR’s vision for urban growth. The measure could accelerate desirable projects, such as infill housing near transit and zero-emission energy infrastructure, but it could also streamline development that contributes to sprawl or environmental harm, including subdivisions on the urban edge and polluting energy facilities,” the organization wrote of its position, which is “No recommendation.”
In a sign of how the measure has scrambled traditional party loyalties, Prop 45 has even split California Republicans, who have long complained about regulations slowing housing production. Steve Hilton, the GOP candidate for governor who advocates building 10 more California cities, largely through the construction of single-family homes in sprawl-like developments, has said supportive things about Prop 45 but hasn’t taken a position. The California Republican Party has endorsed (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) Prop 45, but half a dozen local Republican Party groups oppose it, including the Marin County Republican Party.
Marin County Republican Party Chairman John Turnacliff said his members are worried that Prop 45 could lead to “crony capitalism.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
“Let’s say some big data center developer comes in and takes care of some people in the Legislature with donations, and then all of a sudden they’re pushing for those guys to be qualified for this Proposition 45 benefit of not having to go through all the CEQA stuff, and then they get a fast-track deal,” Turnacliff said.
But other leading CEQA reformers are backing Prop 45, including Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, who wrote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/california-ceqa-20244075.php?utm_campaign=CMS%20Sharing%20Tools%20(Premium)&utm_source=share-by-email&utm_medium=email) a bill signed by Newsom last year that exempted most infill housing projects from the environmental reviews required under CEQA.
“What Prop 45 represents is a thoughtful way to actually get the projects (completed) that are essential for our communities,” Wicks told reporters Monday at a housing-related campaign event for Becerra in El Cerrito. “It still requires (projects) to go through CEQA. It just puts important shot clocks on it.”
Housing Action Coalition, another frequent ally on CEQA reform legislation, is also breaking ranks to back Prop 45. The organization felt that there were gaps in some recent reform legislation in Sacramento — like the ability to quickly build housing on parking lots at dilapidated shopping mall sites — that weren’t covered by existing legislation, said Ali Sapirman, the group’s advocacy and policy manager. Even though the Housing Action Coalition typically doesn’t support legislation that could lead to sprawl, it is confident that existing CEQA laws could be used to stop unwanted sprawl projects.
“And those gaps are real in terms of numbers,” Sapirman said. “The permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home, and that was really critical to our members.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But those gaps weren’t enough to convince other CEQA reformers to back Prop 45.
“There’s a bunch of stuff that 45 could do that we’re like, ‘Well, that would not be a great outcome,’” said California YIMBY’s Lewis. “But there’s some stuff that it would do that could be a good outcome. We weighed those against each other, and we were like, yeah, they kind of cancel each other out. We’re not going to weigh in on this one.”
