Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now (https://insideclimate.fundjournalism.org/donate/?amount=15&campaign=7013a000003Bk97AAC&frequency=monthly)
That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

A central dispute is whether the measure’s provisions for broadband projects could include data centers — an unresolved question legal experts say may ultimately be decided in court.

The community organizer lives in Imperial County, where the nearly 1-million-square-foot facility was proposed. The rural county near the Mexico border struggles with bad air pollution (https://www.niehs.nih.gov/research/supported/translational/community/imperial)and has one of the state’s highest rates of asthma hospitalization for kids, according to the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. One of Salgado’s nephews lives right next to the site and struggles with the respiratory disease.
“It just seemed very unusual that a project of this scale, with that many backup generators, could be permitted without requiring any further [analysis] of what that would mean for residents,” she said.
Advertisement
Now, Salgado and others who share her concern believe Proposition 45 on the November ballot could roll back their wins. The initiative changes the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, a law intended to inform decision makers and the public about a project’s possible environmental impacts — and mitigate them to the extent possible.
Supporters say Proposition 45 will speed up environmental review for essential housing, transportation, water, health, education and other projects, cutting costly delays and passing the savings on to consumers.
Opponents say it not only weakens environmental protections for many developments, but will cover potentially polluting ones — including data centers.
Advertisement
The Yes on 45 campaign rejects the data center claim, but independent legal experts are divided.
At the heart of the debate is the definition of one of the categories covered by Proposition 45: “broadband internet access projects” or “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints.”

Dan Dunmoyer, president and chief executive of the California Building Industry Assn., which supports the proposition, was adamant: “We specifically excluded data centers” when crafting the measure.
Yet the proposition expressly names certain excluded projects such as nuclear energy, high-speed rail and jails. Data centers aren’t among them.
Dunmoyer maintains that even if they’re not explicitly listed, data centers just don’t fit the measure’s definition.
In a Daily Journal op-ed, (https://www.dailyjournal.com/article/393806-california-s-proposition-45-does-not-cover-data-centers) Rachelle Chong, a former Federal Communications Commission member, similarly argues that the definition refers to internet access bought from a provider like AT&T or Comcast. “A conventional data center ordinarily performs an entirely different function,” she wrote, arguing data centers aren’t in play.

But land-use attorneys Matthew McKerley and Richard Frank, in another op-ed, (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) say many modern data centers fit the bill because they house equipment used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet.
They also highlight conspicuous campaign finance contributions, including $250,000 from Prologis, (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484853&view=received) which developed two data centers in San José.
Ethan Elkind, director of the climate program at UC Berkeley Law, said data centers will argue they fit the definition — and then it will be up to the courts to decide.
“Anyone telling you that it’s definitely not going to be data centers, they cannot read the future,” he said. “The way they’ve written the language, they can’t provide 100% assurance.”
Eric Biber, a UC Berkeley law school professor with expertise in environmental law, pointed to language in the measure requiring it to be interpreted broadly “to afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of, and the approval and realization of, essential projects.” In a blog post (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/24/baca-and-data-centers-part-i/), he called it “a thumb on the scale” that could lead courts to conclude that projects should be covered when their eligibility is in doubt.
But Ryan Thomason and J. Scott Miller, partners at the law firm Mitchell Chadwick with CEQA expertise, think it’s likely courts would rule otherwise. However well-intentioned, support for Proposition 45 is deeply misguided.
It is true that California, like most states, needs to build more housing, renewable energy projects, and other 21st century infrastructure.
But eviscerating the California
Environmental Quality Act won't do that.
At its core, CEQA is a "stop, look, and listen" law.
It requires government officials to make informed decisions by considering the environmental impacts of projects, evaluating less impactful alternatives and other ways to mitigate adverse effects, and soliciting public input from affected communities.
CEQA itself cannot prevent projects from going forward, but it can make developers and agencies think harder about designing them in the most sustainable way.

The general concept, as the best-seller of the same name tells us, is to rid public decisions of "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits" — the very public process innovations that have made government more accountable to constituents and significantly reduced air and water pollution.

For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction.
Now Proposition 45 is on the ballot.
Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction.
...
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it.
...
Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance, two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it.
In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles, SPUR, and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions.

If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects.

After Newsom veto, CEQA fight moves from the Capitol to the ballot box
By Andrew Graham
Updated September 30, 2026 8:58 AM
Members of the California Assembly vote during the last day of legislative session at the state Capitol on Monday, Aug. 31, 2026.
ZIYU JULIAN ZHU
julian.zhu@sacbee.com
Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill last week to narrow an exemption to the California Environmental Quality Act for manufacturing facilities. But the long-running political struggle over the cornerstone law continues apace, with both sides now turning their full attention from the Capitol to the voters.
That’s because one of the 14 measures on this year’s ballot would speed up approval under the act for eight categories of building projects — housing and public health developments (such as hospitals); a wide range of clean energy projects; water infrastructure; schools including higher education facilities; public safety projects, including wildfire mitigation work like vegetation management; transportation; and broadband and digital access.
After Newsom’s veto of Senate Bill 954 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317300040.html#storylink=cpy) — an attempt by concerned lawmakers to claw back environmental protections they said the Legislature gave away the year before — the ballot measure is now the primary front in a debate increasingly pitting CEQA’s defenders against both industry representatives and also more moderate Democrat politicians.
The long-simmering debate over CEQA “has become particularly acute and intense” said the bill’s author and Senate Environmental Quality Committee Chair Sen. Catherine Blakespear, D-Encinitas. Blakespear traced the growing fervor over environmental regulations to the 2025 publication of the book“Abundance,” (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/28/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-thompson-dunkelman.html) written by Derek Thompson and Ezra Klein, who has long been considered a deep policy thinker by many moderate Democrats.
Newsom embraced the ideas in that book, as did other California Democrats. Now, Proposition 45 will put questions it raised to voters, testing whether they’re worried enough about California’s economy to change its bedrock environmental policy, at least for some projects. Measure opponents say environmental laws are being blamed for costs of living increases driven by broader economic forces.
“What’s happening is this bigger clash between a desire for the abundance movement to be successful, which is basically the understanding that we need to be delivering the things that people need for our society; housing and internet and transportation and clean energy,” Blakespear said last week, when she joined other lawmakers to speak against Prop. 45. “And then an effort to [scapegoat] environmental laws when the delays and the costs are not typically actually related to the environmental laws. It’s a whole range of reasons that things get delayed, and it’s easier to blame CEQA.”
But proponents point to what they say is mounting evidence of CEQA’s role in slowing the state’s growth, particularly in housing construction. Last week, the Yes on Prop 45 campaign highlighted a study published by the corporate law and lobbying firm Holland & Knight. The study examined 11 years of CEQA lawsuits and concluded that nearly two-thirds of them aimed to slow or block infill development with California towns and cities — where many state policymakers want to see more affordable housing built.
“California cannot solve its housing, infrastructure and affordability challenges if CEQA continues to delay the very projects the state urgently needs,” said the study’s lead author, Holland & Knight attorney Jennifer Hernandez, in a news release from the campaign.
Its backers and architects say Prop. 45 will streamline CEQA review for covered projects by imposing deadlines on agencies and courts to issue approvals or disapprovals. The proposition would put a 365 business-day clock on government agencies to approve or reject a project’s environmental impact report. And on the courts, it would impose a 270-day deadline to resolve any legal challenges brought by project opponents.
Tensions over CEQA have built for years as Californians grapple with housing scarcity, though experts disagree on its exact scale (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/09/california-housing-shortage/), and delays and cost overruns to infrastructure projects that the law’s critics say drive up the high cost of living.
In the Capitol, that tension drove legislation in 2025 to create a series of exemptions for housing and infrastructure development. Newsom put his foot down in that fight, refusing to sign the state budget unless lawmakers passed the exemptions. Blakespear and a large contingent of lawmakers had sought through SB 954 to narrow those exemptions for advanced manufacturing facilities. Seventy-eight Democrats in the Assembly and Senate backed the bill, while a handful of members of the supermajority party withheld their votes and Republicans voted en masse against it.
Opponents, which included a consortium of industrial and business interests including the Bay Area Council, an influential business advocacy group, accused Blakespear of seeking to repeal the exemption before it had a chance to spur development.
Newsom sided with those groups, writing in his veto message that the senator’s bill would have slowed “a long-overdue overhaul to get California building again.”
But Blakespear and her allies didn’t take long to bemoan the bill’s demise. A few days later, she and other lawmakers were speaking against Prop. 45, as a coalition of environmental groups and labor organizations ramps up the campaign against the measure.
The lawmakers said the measure, which runs 41 pages and would apply to eight fairly broad categories of building projects deemed essential, is CEQA’s opponents seeking to take a cudgel to an act that should at best be tweaked carefully in Sacramento. Blakespear pointed to four recent bills she said lawmakers passed to ease the approval of housing.
“We are actually working in the Legislature to promote what we want, and this just goes way too far,” she said.
Loading…
But some lawmakers do support the measure. Perhaps most notable was an endorsement in February from Assembly Appropriations Chair Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. The lawmaker has been a driver of bills to spur housing construction, and at one point in the legislative session, SB 954’s backers worried she’d use her powerful committee chairmanship to kill the bill (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316707439.html). Wicks ultimately voted in favor of the bill after policy implications to housing construction were amended out.
“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” Wicks said when backing Prop 45.
So far, the public polling on the measure’s popularity with voters hasn’t been definitive. In late June and early July, 73% of likely voters told pollsters for the Public Policy Institute of California they’d vote yes on a proposal to expedite CEQA reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. But, those polling numbers changed (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317256476.html) earlier this month when PPIC again asked voters about the measure, this time using language closer to what will be on the ballot in November.
In that poll, only a slim majority, 49%, of likely voters said they’d vote yes, while 46% said no and 5% said they were undecided.
“It is clear that once voters learn exactly what this measure does — allowing developers to fast-track polluting projects like data centers in communities across California, lowering our state’s defenses to Trump’s attack on clean air and water and then sticking us with the bill — the more they sour on it,” said the No on Prop 45 campaign in a statement highlighting the sharply lower support.
The measures proponents have accused the No campaign of trying to scare voters away from what they describe as a limited set of rule changes designed to ease approvals for only projects in the public interest.
“The opponents have been shamelessly dishonest in stoking fears over the ballot measure’s impact on California’s natural resources and the health of our communities. They want to distract voters from the fact that Prop. 45 is a change in government process, not environmental protection,” said California Chamber of Commerce President Jennifer Barrera in a blog post.
The two sides have clashed vehemently over whether the measure would apply to data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316801972.html#storylink=cpy), which are extremely politically unpopular projects.

The end of endangered species habitat protections in California?
Not quite, but the combination of the Trump Admin and Prop 45 will drastically reduce protections.
California likes to portray itself as an environmental leader, and in many ways it is. But in the context of one of the most important areas of environmental law – protecting endangered species – California is on the verge of eliminating most of its protections for the habitat of endangered species. That is the result of the double-punch of retrenchment by the Trump Administration on the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA), and the impacts of the likely passage of Proposition 45 this fall.
First, why habitat protections for endangered species matters. There are many different threats to endangered species globally, in the US, and in California. Climate change, invasive species, overhunting or over collection. But one of the most important ones is the destruction of endangered species habitat. While many laws, including California’s Endangered Species Act (CESA) protect against hunting and harvesting of endangered plants and animals, protecting individual plants and animals from direct take is only of limited benefit of those plants and animals do not have habitat to occupy. And that is what is under threat right now.
I’ll begin at the federal level. As I noted in prior (https://legal-planet.org/2025/04/23/whats-the-harm/) blog (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/25/harming-species/) posts (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/19/in-harms-way-2/) the Trump Administration is trying to repeal the definition of harm in the regulations implementing the ESA – that matters because it is that regulatory definition that extends protections under Section 9 of the ESA to endangered species habitat. Section 9 applies to federal, state, local, and private actors, and prohibits “take” of endangered species, which the statute defines to include “harm.” This regulatory definition has been in place since the early 1980s, so the changes are a big deal.
There are other protections for endangered species habitat under the ESA, but those too have been, or are being, trimmed back substantially. Section 7 of the ESA prohibits federal agencies from “adversely modifying” areas designated as “critical habitat” for endangered species. As part of the regulatory revisions by the Trump Administration, the Administration is also trying to make it easier to exclude areas from critical habitat (https://legal-planet.org/2026/01/03/ping-pong-government-and-the-esa/) based on economic or other factors. That would substantially narrow the application of Section 7’s protections.
On top of that, since Section 7 and the adverse modification prohibition only apply to federal actions, Section 7 does not cover private development activity unless there is a federal permit. Historically one of the federal permit requirements most likely to trigger Section 7 and ensure endangered species habitat protection was wetlands protection under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. That mattered in part because we have lost a lot of wetlands in the United States. But the Supreme Court in Sackett dramatically cut back on the scope of wetlands protection a few years ago, and the Trump Administration is seeking to (https://legal-planet.org/2026/01/03/stuck-in-the-swamp/) aggressively extend (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/climate/epa-wetlands-water-protections.html) those restrictions on wetlands protection.
But surely California, being at the forefront of environmental law, can fill the breach. Won’t California’s own Endangered Species Act (CESA) protect that habitat?
The answer to that question is . . . very unclear. As I’ve noted before (https://legal-planet.org/2021/10/14/reforming-the-california-endangered-species-act/), CESA on its face does not explicitly protect habitat of endangered species – it only explicitly prohibits killing or injuring individual members of listed species. Whether that includes habitat modification has long been contested, and probably varies in practice with the specific activity and particular species at issue in any given case.
But there is a different California law that does provide stringent protections for endangered species habitat in California: the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). It applies to all government actions in California, and because of the ubiquity of land-use regulation in California, that covers most private development as well. CEQA requires analysis and feasible mitigation for significant impacts to endangered species habitat. So we’re all good?
Not so fast. As I’ve also written about, Proposition 45 will likely pass in November, and it would likely eliminate protections for endangered species habitat under CEQA (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) for a wide range of projects (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/), including housing, freeways, clean energy, mass transit, dams, irrigation projects, timber harvesting, and potentially any development activity that converts natural habitat in California (because that might reduce fire risk). So the backstop of CEQA protections may well be gone after November.
What will be left? Some protections, but they will be much more patchwork, and uncertain as to the extent to which they cover individual species.
First, protected areas remain, like parks, wildlife refuges, and areas managed by land trusts. But those are uneven in the extent to which they cover endangered species. For instance, high-altitude mountain habitats are well covered with federal land in wilderness protections in the Sierra Nevada, but grassland habitats in the Central Valley have very little protected areas.
Second, the adverse modification provisions of Section 7 will still apply for federally listed species with critical habitat. But that is only some listed species (a significant proportion still have no designated critical habitat) and a lot of private development activity in California may not be covered by Section 7 post-Sackett.
Third, there are other state laws that protect habitat for some particular species, such as Joshua trees, but that is only a fraction of all endangered species in the state.
Fourth, there are other state laws that limit development on certain kinds of lands – for instance, California has broader wetlands protections than under the Clean Water Act, and also has a regulatory program restricting development that affects state waterways. But it will be happenstance whether those laws protect the habitat for a particular endangered species.
Fifth, it’s possible CESA might be interpreted by state agencies and the courts as generally applying to habitat destruction for CESA-listed species. (Note that this would not help the many species listed only under the ESA, but not under CESA.) And even short of that, state agencies and the courts might interpret the prohibition on killing or injuring CESA-listed species as including unintentional killing or injury, such as habitat development that also directly kills or injures a member of a CESA-listed species. (Consider bulldozing endangered plant species to construct a development project – the bulldozing would kill or injure the plants, but not intentionally (i.e., the intent was to develop the project, not kill the plants).) That would provide protections for relatively immobile species (think plants or shellfish), but would provide much less protection for mobile, large-range species (think mountain lions).
Finally, as I’ve noted (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/19/in-harms-way-2/), the Trump Administration’s attempt to repeal the harm definition is legally vulnerable, and could be overturned in court.
Come 2027, the state that claims to be a leader in environmental law may have ended up gutting a core component of its environmental law protections for endangered species.
And I’m not particularly optimistic that the legislature will step in. The CEQA reforms in 2025 that exempted some housing projects from CEQA review allowed those exemptions to apply for projects on endangered species habitat (https://legal-planet.org/2025/09/10/clean-up-on-aisle-131/), and the Assembly Appropriations Committee (chaired by East Bay Democrat Buffy Wicks) blocked an effort to change that this year (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/08/ceqa-reform-advanced-manufacturing-sb954/).

Prop 45 Streamlines approvals to build essential projects faster and make California more affordable
Last updated: October 12, 2026
The Problem
California's cost of living is out of control. Our outdated system for approving housing, water projects, schools and hospitals (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) is too slow—and it's driving up the cost of living for all of us.
$75,000+ (https://yesonprop45.com/cost-of-delay-per-home/) added to every new home, which drives up rents and mortgages.
Billions added in taxpayer and consumer costs (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) for hospitals, roads and clean energy projects.
Delayed progress on critical environmental projects to reduce pollution, prevent wildfires (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-11-25/cal-fire-approach-to-socals-wildfire-crisis-could-make-things-worse-court-says) and cut emissions.
See real California projects delayed for years (https://yesonprop45.com/case-studies/) →
The Solution
Prop 45 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) cuts red tape and unnecessary delays so California can build the essential infrastructure we need faster, lower our cost of living and improve our quality of life.
Including:
Clean water infrastructure
Clean Energy
Housing
Roads, bridges, and transit
Hospitals and health care facilities
Schools and educational facilities
Wildfire prevention
Broadband infrastructure
What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.
Why California Needs Prop 45
Prop 45 Fixes California’s Broken Approval System
Rising housing costs, soaring electricity bills and crumbling infrastructure are making California more expensive. Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:
Clean drinking water and supply projects
Hospitals, clinics and other health care facilities
Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters In summary Prop. 45, billed as a pro-housing development measure, may have the unintended consequence of making it easier to build data centers, opponents say. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters considering Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-45-yimby/) will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless. That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) at the city and county level. Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45. Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), like housing and schools, and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny. Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends. “What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added. MORE ON DATA CENTERS California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) October 22, 2026 October 22, 2026 Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges. “The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887), which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers. Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/) ad other infrastructure like roads and bridges. Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers. Amelia Matier, from the Yes on 45 campaign, echoed that take, saying, “Data centers are not included in Prop 45.” She added: “The defenders of California’s unaffordable status quo are desperate to distract voters with lies because they cannot defend the costly delays and red tape driving up prices for working families. ” Opponents of the measure include the California Labor Federation, Western Center on Law & Poverty, and various environmental advocacy groups that have spent more than $31 million dollars pushing back against the measure. Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-45-modifies-environmental-review-certain-projects-initiative-statute) behind its passage. Proponents have poured over $40 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/09/new-california-laws-data-centers/) aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review. Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) in their communities. I've got the core picture now, so next I'm weighing the strongest arguments on the supporting side: the Blue Sky Consulting estimate of about 20,000 homes a year, the Holland & Knight study, the Little Hoover Commission report, and the Livermore Eden Housing example. I'm also noting the Hanson Bridgett letter that argues it doesn't weaken environmental law, and the labor question, since the Building Trades are opposed even though the yes side frames it differently.

I'm going to check the Hanson Bridgett letter and the Blue Sky report to see what the yes side's analysis rests on. After that I need to settle how to answer the user's yes-or-no question on this contested ballot measure.

I'm weighing whether to pick a side on this contested measure at all, since the answer turns on how someone values environmental review against faster building. Expert groups, the Democrats, labor, and business interests are split on it, so a flat yes or no would hide that. I'm leaning toward giving a brief, even-handed answer that explains the tradeoff rather than choosing for the user.

I'm weighing whether a one-word yes or no is the right answer here, since this is a contested ballot measure where the arguments split on how someone values environmental review against faster building. Given that, I'm inclined to explain the main tradeoffs and a simple guide for which values point toward each vote, rather than choose for the user. The case for yes has real problems to address, since CEQA is widely criticized for delays and for being used to block projects.

I'm laying out the other side now: the case against this measure, weighing whether its environmental-review concerns outweigh the speed gains.

I'm now going through the case against the measure: its scope reaches well beyond housing to freeways, greenfield subdivisions, dams, and logging, and some legal experts argue it substantially narrows judicial review, limits the alternatives analysis, and restricts remedies. I also see that it leaves out many California tribes that aren't federally recognized, and caps public comment in a way that excludes late submissions.

I'm noting that the measure would be hard to amend, needing a two-thirds legislative vote, and only to further its own purposes. I also see that the 2025 infill housing exemption already exists, so the remaining housing gains are mostly on greenfield and large sites, while the LAO estimates costs in the tens of millions to over $100 million a year at first. The opposition list includes the state Democratic Party, labor, environmental groups, and several newspapers.

I'm settling on a guide rather than a single word, since reasonable people weigh environmental review against faster building differently. The PPIC polling is close to split, and even pro-housing groups disagree, so I'll lay out the tradeoffs and let the user's priorities decide.

I'm settling on not giving a one-word verdict here, since this is a contested value question and it isn't my place to tell the user how to vote. I'll give a balanced breakdown of the tradeoffs and a quick guide so they can weigh it by their own priorities.

I'm going to check the Hanson Bridgett letter and the Legislative Counsel opinion on data centers, and see whether any neutral analysis disputes the "objective existing laws" reading of the measure.

Proposition 45, Its Implementation, and Its Benefits To Public Agencies
Proposition 45, its Implementation, and Its Benefits to Public Agencies
Clarification of Impacts of CEQA Reform on Cities and Counties
July 30, 2026
Proposition 45 has raised many questions among stakeholders, including public agencies. To dispel some confusion about how the new law would operate, Hanson Bridgett drafted the letter, below, to help public agencies understand how Proposition 45 would affect their operations, including how it would help these agencies process applications for schools, hospitals, housing, and other essential projects.
To: Interested Parties
Re: Prop. 45 – Local Control and CEQA Litigation Considerations
Hanson Bridgett is representing the California Chamber of Commerce with regard to the proposed Affordable California Act initiative measure, Proposition 45 (Prop. 45). Our firm has many decades of experience in representing local governments on land use matters and a variety of public agencies undertaking significant infrastructure projects, including defending such projects against challenges under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). I have personally advised public agencies for more than 30 years on infrastructure and development projects.
I have reviewed Prop. 45 with particular attention to its impact on local land use authority and municipal litigation exposure under CEQA. Based on my review, Prop. 45 would not limit an agency’s discretion to approve, deny, or condition a project. While the measure makes changes to the manner in which local governments process what it defines as “essential projects,” it provides valuable public benefits in clarifying the environmental review process and in limiting CEQA litigation.
Some of these benefits will be financial and significant. While agencies recover most costs for private development from the applicants — which won’t change under Prop. 45 — agencies do not have this option with public projects, including programmatic land use plans, public infrastructure projects, and publicly subsidized development such as affordable housing.
Administrative and judicial delays can consume years of staff time, require extensive consultant and outside counsel support, delay critical public infrastructure, and expose taxpayers to escalating costs. With private projects, costs can be recovered from applicants, but time cannot. With streamlined approval and less litigation risk, the time agency staff expends on continuing hearings and preparing administrative records can be better spent on programs that improve the community.
California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) echoed these points, concluding that Prop. 45 “could reduce the ongoing number of CEQA lawsuits” and that local governments could realize savings through smaller administrative records, reduced litigation demands, and limitations on courts’ ability to rescind a project’s approval. The LAO further noted that faster environmental reviews could help state and local governments avoid inflationary cost increases on public infrastructure projects.
With Prop. 45, cities and counties gain tools to deliver essential public infrastructure more efficiently, improve predictability, and reduce taxpayer costs associated with prolonged project delivery. With private projects, local governments will retain full discretion to approve, disapprove, and condition projects while having better certainty their decisions will not be overturned in court, and without having to overwhelm staff with tasks related to challenges, like the preparation of administrative records.
Local Control Is Preserved
Prop. 45 does not transfer land use authority away from cities or counties. It is a purely procedural streamlining measure that does not require any city to approve a project, create any new right to challenge a project denial, or exempt projects from CEQA review. Local governments retain full discretion to determine the appropriate level of CEQA review, approve, condition, or deny projects, apply zoning and general plan policies, require mitigation measures and technical studies, and impose permit conditions necessary to address local impacts. Local governments also retain authority to adopt new standards and requirements for future projects.
Prop. 45 requires projects to be evaluated using the standards local governments themselves establish. Local governments may rely on any applicable statute, regulation, ordinance, policy, or standard in effect when the application is submitted including standards governing density, height, setbacks, design, noise, traffic, open space, and other local development criteria. Prop. 45 does not limit the substantive standards a city may apply; it simply requires agencies to apply the laws that are in place when an application is submitted. Local governments may also apply subsequently adopted requirements necessary to address a life-safety impact. In short, local governments continue to decide what gets built and under what conditions.
Prop. 45 also preserves local cost recovery. Local governments may continue charging applicants for staff time, consultant expenses, and other project review costs, just as they do today.
Many projects eligible for streamlining — including housing, transportation improvements, fire stations, water infrastructure, schools, healthcare facilities, and broadband projects — are projects local governments frequently sponsor and deliver themselves. When acting as both lead agency and project applicant, local governments retain flexibility to extend review timelines while benefiting from the measure’s litigation protections. A city or county also will have more certainty a responsible agency (e.g., LAFCO, utility provider, resource agency), considering and making determinations about a project that local government wants, will act quickly.
Prop. 45 Strengthens Legal Protections for Local Governments
Under current law, a local government’s decision to approve a project may be challenged by third-parties, many of whom use litigation as a delay tactic to make projects more expensive and less likely to be built. CEQA lawsuits often take years to resolve, imposing significant costs on local governments through prolonged staff commitments, consultant expenses, outside counsel fees, and delayed delivery of public infrastructure. In some cases, the cost and uncertainty of litigation can jeopardize important public projects regardless of the merits of the claims. Prop. 45 reduces the time, cost, and uncertainty associated with CEQA litigation through several targeted reforms:
Common-sense limits on late CEQA comments. Public comment participation is a legal prerequisite to any CEQA lawsuit and local governments must respond to each comment submitted. Some project opponents exploit this requirement by submitting lengthy comments on the eve of a project’s public hearing. Prop. 45 establishes firm public comment periods of 20 days for NDs/MNDs and 45 days for draft EIRs. These periods may not be extended (except by a court), and late comments are excluded from the record except where they could not reasonably have been raised earlier due to project changes or new information. This preserves meaningful public participation while saving agency staff late nights responding to eleventh-hour comments, as well as the time and inconvenience of holding multiple, continued hearings and preparing staff reports and other materials for these purposes. Prop. 45 thereby reduces abuse of the comment process.
30-day statute of limitations. CEQA challenges must be filed within 30 days of the Notice of Determination or Notice of Exemption, allowing local governments to achieve legal certainty sooner.
270-day judicial resolution. CEQA actions, including appeals, generally must be resolved within 270 calendar days. Replacing multi-year litigation with a defined judicial timeline has the potential to save local governments years of delay and substantial legal expense.
Substantial evidence standard. Courts must uphold local decisions supported by substantial evidence, reinforcing deference to local government decisions and making it less likely that locally approved projects will be overturned based on competing interpretations of the record.
Targeted remedies. If a court identifies a deficiency, the remedy is limited to correcting the specific error rather than vacating the entire project approval. This protection will spare local governments from repeating years of environmental review and incurring substantial additional costs to restart project reviews.
Taken together, these provisions provide local governments with meaningful legal protections designed to narrow disputes, expedite their resolution, reduce administrative burdens, and protect taxpayers from the significant costs associated with prolonged CEQA litigation. While it may require some additional effort from cities and counties at the beginning, the benefits will be considerable over time, both to local governments and communities as a whole.
Conclusion
Prop. 45 preserves local control while providing local governments with meaningful legal protections designed to reduce litigation-related delays, improve predictability, and protect taxpayers from the substantial costs associated with prolonged CEQA disputes. While it does impose changes in how local governments process a variety of project approvals, it will make the consideration of many projects more efficient and less costly, adding to the quality of life for the citizens of our state.
Very truly yours,
Michael N. Conneran

I. Executive Summary
Proposition 45 Overview
Proposition 45 (the “Building an Affordable California Act”) would reform state laws governing the review and approval of certain construction projects in California, including new homes, educational, public health, and public safety facilities, and expansions of transportation, clean energy, and broadband infrastructure (i.e., “essential projects”). This report provides estimates of the economic and fiscal impacts that Prop 45 would generate in California.
Under current law, the approval timeline for essential projects can last several years, resulting in higher construction costs and reduced investment in housing and infrastructure. Prop 45 would reduce review period delays by establishing binding time limits on these review phases and by introducing further procedural reforms related to environmental review litigation, late-filed public comments, and the analysis of project alternatives. Reducing these delays under Prop 45 would result in more housing, lower construction costs, and significant savings for taxpayers and ratepayers.
Prop 45’s Estimated Impacts on Housing, Taxpayers and Ratepayers
Nearly 20,000 additional homes annually. Prop 45’s approval timeline reductions will increase annual housing permitting by 18.1%, or nearly 20,000 additional homes per year, resulting in nearly 200,000 additional homes over ten years.
$774 million in total annual savings on non-residential construction costs. Across both publicly and privately sponsored essential non-residential projects, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce costs by $774 million annually.
Approximately $1.5 billion annually in combined savings and additional revenues for state and local governments and other public agencies. Over the 10-year period following Prop 45’s implementation, the measure’s residential and non-residential impacts are estimated to generate $1.5 billion annually, on average, in additional tax revenues and fiscal savings, including:
$1.1 billion in state and local tax revenues from increased residential construction, and
$386 million in annual savings for public works project sponsors, including $238 million in transportation projects, $73 million in water projects and $52 million in educational facilities.
$250 million in annual savings for California ratepayers. Prop 45’s impact on clean energy project costs is estimated to save California ratepayers $250 million annually.
Prop 45’s Estimated Impact on CEQA Review Timelines
Under current law, EIR reviews take approximately three years. Prop 45’s time limits would reduce delays related to project reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). For residential projects requiring an Environmental Impact Report (EIR), as shown in Figure 1, the CEQA review period lasts 1,141 days (3.1 years), on average, under current law; non-residential EIR review periods average 1,101 days (3.0 years).
Most EIR reviews exceed Prop 45’s time limit. Under current law, 59% of residential EIRs and 56% of non-residential EIRs take longer than the 591-day maximum review period established by Prop 45.
Prop 45 would cut the average EIR timeline in half. Due to the enforcement of Prop 45’s 591-day limit on EIR certifications, the average EIR review period would decline by 639 days for residential EIRs and 603 days for non-residential EIRs.
Prop 45 would make EIR timelines more predictable. Under current law, roughly 17% of EIR reviews last longer than five years (see Figure 1). By capping this period at 591 days, Prop 45 reduces this review period uncertainty. Among the residential EIRs exceeding this time limit, the average review period was 1,674 days (4.6 years); under Prop 45, these projects’ average review period would decline by 1,082 days or roughly three years.
Non-EIR project reviews would also be completed more quickly. Projects receiving Mitigated Negative Declarations (MNDs), Negative Declarations (NDs) or CEQA exemptions currently have estimated average review periods of six to eight months. Depending on review type, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce these timelines by one to two months.

Other Prop 45 reforms would further reduce review period delays. In addition to its CEQA review period limits, Prop 45 also establishes time limits for other phases of project review, including 30 days for application completeness, 135 days for other discretionary approvals following CEQA review, and 300 days for judicial review. The measure also includes procedural reforms related to streamlined analysis of project alternatives, late-filed public comments, and judicial review. The economic and fiscal estimates in this report quantify only the impacts of Prop 45’s CEQA review timelines and therefore represent conservative lower-bound estimates. They do not include potential impacts from these additional timeline and procedural reforms.
Impact of Prop 45 Timelines on Residential Construction Activity
Residential permitting would increase by 18.1% under Prop 45. As shown in Figure 2, based on Prop 45’s estimated impact on CEQA review timelines, the measure would increase annual permitting rates by an estimated 18.1%, or nearly 20,000 additional homes annually. The largest increase occurs among EIR projects, which account for 23.4% of units permitted under the status quo; EIR housing starts are estimated to increase 36.1%. Increases among the non-EIR project types range from 6.5% to 13.9%.

Prop 45’s impact on the statewide housing supply is estimated to reduce housing costs by 0.66% after ten years. Over the 10-year period following Prop 45’s implementation, given the estimated increase in annual permitting, the measure would increase California’s housing stock by nearly 200,000 units, or 1.21%. This additional supply is estimated to reduce housing costs by 0.66% relative to status quo trends.
Over a ten-year period, the construction of new homes under Prop 45 would generate $1.1 billion of tax revenue annually for state and local governments. As shown in Figure 3, the increase in homebuilding would produce an estimated $315 million annually for the State General Fund and $168 million annually for local governments in construction period tax revenues (i.e., personal income taxes, corporation taxes, and sales taxes). Impacts of Prop 45 Timelines on Non-Residential Construction Costs
By reducing delay, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce non-residential EIR project costs by 3%, on average. Due to construction cost inflation and the cost of pre-development stage capital, review period delays increase public agency construction costs by 1.34% to 1.95% per year of delay (depending on the essential project category) and private sector costs by 1.70% to 4.95% per year. Under Prop 45, the estimated 1.65-year reduction in average EIR timelines would therefore generate per-project cost reductions of 2.22% to 3.22% for public agencies and 2.81% to 8.17% for investor-owned utilities (IOUs) and other private sector sponsors. On average, across all EIR projects, costs would decline by an estimated 3.0% under Prop 45. The measure would also reduce costs on non-EIR projects.
Non-residential cost reductions under Prop 45 would generate annual savings of $774 million. An estimated $49.4 billion is spent annually on essential non-residential projects in California. As shown in Figure 4, given Prop 45’s estimated impacts on EIR and non-EIR project costs, the measure would generate an estimated $774 million in annual construction cost savings, including $386 million for public agencies, $250 million in clean-energy project savings accruing to California ratepayers, and $137 million for other private essential-project sponsors.

II. Prop 45 Overview
Prop 45’s provisions fall into two broad categories: binding time limits controlling the duration essential project review periods (“timeline provisions”), and procedural reforms that provide options for simplifying a project’s environmental review and any related litigation (“procedural reforms”). 1
Application receipt to application completeness (30+ Days)
Within 30 calendar days of the submission of an essential project application, Prop 45 requires the public agency to determine whether the application is complete. Applicants have 90 days to amend and resubmit applications that are determined incomplete.
Application completeness to CEQA Determination (90 – 591 Days)
Once an application is deemed complete, any environmental review conducted by a lead agency under CEQA is subject to a CEQA review time limit that varies according to the type of CEQA review conducted. Prop 45 requires that EIR certification decisions be made within 365 business days (531 calendar days) of application completeness. 2 For projects receiving a mitigated negative declaration (MND) or Negative Declaration (ND), this determination must be made within 180 business days (262 calendar days) of application completeness. Notices of a project’s exemption from CEQA are required within 90 business days (131 calendar days).
If the lead agency fails to comply with the applicable CEQA review time limit, the applicant may request a public hearing. Within 60 calendar days of this request, the lead agency must complete its CEQA review and issue its determination. As a result, under Prop 45, the maximum timeline for an EIR certification, for example, would generally be 591 days (i.e., 531 days for the certification of an EIR plus this 60-day noncompliance period), while the maximum timeline for an Exempt project is 191 days.
Other Entitlement (135 days)
In addition to CEQA review, essential projects may also require other discretionary approvals. Under Prop 45, the public agencies responsible for these other entitlements must provide approvals within 90 calendar days of the completion of CEQA review. Because agencies that fail to meet this deadline must act within 45 days of an essential project applicant’s written request, Prop 45 effectively limits this review period to 135 days.
Litigation (300 days)
Prop 45 requires that legal challenges brought against essential projects be filed within 30 days of a lead agency’s CEQA determination and that courts resolve this litigation within 270 days using judicial streamlining procedures available for certain projects under existing state law. A summary of Prop 45’s time limits for each phase of essential project review is shown in Figure 5.

III. Residential Impacts
Project carrying costs, including interest on loans, land holding costs, consultant and legal fees, and construction cost inflation, accrue throughout the entitlement process, and incremental increases in these costs reduce project feasibility, causing projects to be delayed, downsized, or abandoned. Timeline uncertainty compounds this effect, as lenders and investors are more likely to advance projects when entitlement durations are predictable. The expected review timeline reductions under Prop 45 would therefore increase the number of financially feasible projects and raise rates of residential development. 3
Entitlement Time and Entitlement Volatility Elasticity
Prior studies of residential project review periods and development feasibility in California show that development activity is responsive to changes in both the average duration of the entitlement review period as well as changes in the uncertainty (or “volatility”) of this timeline.
Entitlement Time Elasticity
The entitlement time elasticity refers to the extent to which a reduction in the average duration of a project’s entitlement review generates an increase in the rate of homebuilding. Two prior studies in California have estimated this elasticity. First, a Terner Center analysis of housing project feasibility (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/policy-dashboard-los-angeles/) assessed the impacts of various reforms of local zoning rules and entitlement procedures on the number of residential units developed in Los Angeles County. 4 Terner’s findings are based on model pro formas that were developed for each residential parcel in Los Angeles County based on the parcel’s location, status quo zoning designation, and empirical estimates of the costs incurred by developers during each phase of entitlement, permitting, and construction. The Terner analysis finds that a 25% reduction in entitlement timelines would be expected to increase annual housing starts by 9.8% (i.e., an entitlement period elasticity estimate of 0.392). 5 Consistent with the Terner Center’s finding, Gabriel and Kung’s (2024) analysis (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4873581) of City of Los Angeles entitlement and permitting data over the 2010-2022 period showed that a 25% reduction in average multifamily project approval time increased the number of residential units permitted annually by 11.4% (i.e., an approval time elasticity of 0.46). 6
For purposes of estimating Prop 45’s impact on residential EIR project development, this report conservatively adopts the Terner Center’s entitlement time elasticity of 0.39.
Entitlement Volatility Elasticity
In addition to the average entitlement duration, entitlement time uncertainty is itself a significant factor affecting residential project feasibility, as investors and developers require larger returns to compensate for added project risks. Gabriel and Kung quantify this uncertainty based on the standard deviation of the natural log of multifamily project approval times and refer to this measure as approval time “volatility.” 7 Based on multifamily development data in Los Angeles, the authors find that a decline of 25% in this log-form standard deviation increases residential project starts by 8.5% (i.e., a volatility elasticity of 0.327).

I won't give a one-word yes or no on this one. After looking into it, the choice comes down to which risks and goals matter more to you, and well-informed people disagree. Even pro-housing groups that have pushed CEQA reform for years stayed neutral, including California YIMBY, YIMBY Action and SPUR. I don't think it's my place to tell you how to vote, so here's a summary to help you decide.

**What Prop 45 does**
- **Who it covers:** It creates an optional fast track through CEQA, the state's environmental review law, for "essential" projects. That includes nearly all housing (suburban subdivisions too), water, clean energy and transmission lines, hospitals, schools, fire and police stations, wildfire work, broadband, and roads, highways and transit. Related infrastructure is covered too. Jails, new oil and gas production, high-speed rail and the Delta tunnel are excluded.
- **Deadlines:** Agencies get about 1.5 years to finish a full environmental impact report. Lawsuits must be filed within 30 days and decided within 270.
- **Narrower review:** The developer proposes just one alternative to study, alongside the project and a "no project" option. Impacts are judged only against the rules in place when the application is filed. Public comment periods are capped. Only federally recognized tribes must be consulted.
- **Narrower lawsuits:** Courts can halt only the flawed part of a project, never cancel its approval.
- **Hard to change:** The Legislature would need a two-thirds vote to amend it.
- **Cost:** The state's Legislative Analyst's Office estimates early government costs in the high tens of millions to over $100 million a year, partly covered by fees. The long-term effect could be positive or negative.

**Best case for Yes**
- Delays and lawsuits under CEQA really do raise costs. Even Berkeley law professor Eric Biber, a sharp critic of the measure, agrees it targets real problems: shifting standards, endless re-studies, and lawsuits filed just to delay.
- It would speed up projects that the 2025 exemption for urban "infill" housing doesn't reach, like transmission lines, water projects, hospitals and big redevelopment sites.
- A study paid for by the measure's backers estimates about 20,000 more homes a year. The same study projects housing costs only about 0.7% lower after 10 years.
- **Backers include:** the California Chamber of Commerce, homebuilders, hospitals, the Farm Bureau, NAACP California/Hawaii, LULAC, clean-energy groups, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks and the state Republican Party. The Yes campaign counts 28 newspaper endorsements, including the Mercury News, Sacramento Bee and San Diego Union-Tribune.

**Best case for No**
- It's much broader than "essential" suggests. It covers freeway expansions, new subdivisions on undeveloped land including fire zones, and dams.
- It may also cover data centers. The Yes side cites a legal opinion saying it doesn't, but several law professors think it likely does.
- Environmental law experts at Berkeley and UCLA say it largely guts CEQA for covered projects, since the developer picks the alternative and courts can't stop a poorly studied project.
- Most urban infill housing was already exempted in 2025, so much of the added housing benefit would go to suburban sprawl.
- Mistakes would be hard to fix because of the two-thirds rule.
- **Opponents include:** the California Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, Sierra Club, American Lung Association, major labor unions and the SF Chronicle. Governor Newsom hasn't taken a position.

**How to decide**
- **Lean yes** if you think permit delays are a major reason California is so expensive, and you'll accept less environmental review and public input in exchange for faster building across the board.
- **Lean no** if you're more worried about sprawl, freeways, wildlife habitat, data centers or tribal input. Same if you'd rather the Legislature make targeted fixes that are easier to adjust later.

The latest statewide poll (PPIC, Oct. 16–22) had it at 46% yes and 50% no.
